Vendor docs describe a CLI sandbox that blocks sensitive files like ~/.ssh and .env and hides anything not explicitly mounted. They also describe Git-worktree isolation and Deny/Ask/Allow permission lists. Independent reports concretely contradict this: an indirect prompt-injection attack got the agent past its own default setting to read .env and exfiltrate the data, the default network allowlist included webhook.site as an exfiltration vector, and in one incident an agent auto-executed a command that wiped a whole drive. Missing for 10: documented network-egress sandboxing, sandbox coverage for the IDE/desktop agent (not just the CLI), in-depth sandbox docs, and independent confirmation that isolation holds against prompt injection.

Cursor Automations run cloud agents in the background on a schedule. Schedules use preset options or cron expressions, alongside event triggers from GitHub, GitLab, Slack, webhooks and Linear. Cursor Automations are documented, but they are created through the Agents Window, cursor.com/automations, the /automate skill or Marketplace templates, and no evidence shows version history, change review or rollback for them. Only adjacent automation configuration lives in files that git can version and PRs can review: skills are described as "version-controlled packages", and hooks.json, project rules and project-level CLI permission files sit in the project. missing for 10: versioning of Automations themselves, a review/approval flow for automation changes, rollback to a prior automation version, and hands-on corroboration.

Cursor's Cloud Agents run in isolated VMs with full development environments, work in parallel on tasks "for hours or days" without the local machine being connected, and can be launched from the IDE, web, Slack, Linear, the Cloud Agents API, or the SDK's Cloud runtime, which is built for runs that survive the caller disconnecting. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that long-running background cloud runs work as documented.

Cursor documents several layers of tool-access control. Enterprise admins can control which MCP servers users may run from the dashboard, and servers can be toggled on and off. Run Modes offer an Allowlist mode covering shell, MCP and Fetch calls, CLI permission tokens gate Shell/Read/Write, and hooks such as beforeMCPExecution/preToolUse can block tool calls. Custom subagents can also be given restricted tool access. Missing for 10: detailed docs on how the admin MCP allowlist works (only a one-line claim), explicit admin controls over first-party integrations such as Slack/Linear/GitHub, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

Cloud Agents run in cloud VMs and do not need your local machine to stay connected. Missing for 10: explicit documentation of handing off a local IDE/CLI session to another device, clear docs on continuing an existing agent's conversation from the web or mobile app, and independent or hands-on corroboration of cross-device continuation.

Nothing documents the agent automatically building or recalling memories on its own. Missing for 10: a documented automatic memory feature, agent-generated memories that persist across sessions, automatic recall/retrieval of past-session context, and hands-on corroboration.

Cursor's docs describe Agent Skills as an open standard for giving agents specialized capabilities.
